title: Consonantal i is written j
decision: Write consonantal i as j in all Latin, quotations included: jam, ejus, major, conjungō, Jōannēs.
html: The lexicon writes consonantal i as j, as Lewis & Short does, and as the editor’s own Latin readers do. Between vowels j was pronounced double, so the syllable before it is heavy while its vowel is short (rejice scans heavy although re- is short, Verg. Ecl. 3.96): major, ejus, pejus therefore carry no macron, while long prefixes keep theirs (dējectus, prōjēcit). The letter stays i where it is a vowel: in the interjection iō, in forms of eō (iērunt, adiērunt), in superior, interior, Plēiades, in Iūlus where Vergil makes it three syllables, and after qu and gu (quiēs, reliquiae). Citation labels keep each dictionary’s own headword. Search treats i and j alike.

history.html: Adopted, to match the editor’s own Latin readers.
pejerō is written without a macron, by the rule for the vowel before an intervocalic j: its pe- is not a long prefix (Lewis & Short pējĕro, from per-jūrō).

title: Macrons are spelling
decision: Mark every long vowel, fully and consistently, as part of the spelling.
html: Macrons are treated like the accents of French: part of the word, not an aid for beginners. Short vowels are left plain, and a heavy syllable is not by itself a long vowel. Hidden quantities, long vowels in syllables already heavy by position, are marked too (rēctus, cīnctus).

title: Which authority settles a vowel
decision: Lewis & Short first; Bennett for hidden quantities that Lewis & Short leaves unmarked; de Vaan wherever he explicitly discusses the vowel.
html: Lewis & Short marks most quantities but leaves many hidden ones blank, and Bennett’s study of hidden quantity fills those gaps. De Vaan’s Etymological Dictionary of Latin and the other Italic Languages (2008) is the most recent of the three, so where he discusses a vowel he takes precedence (sāriō). Where the authorities conflict, the entry says which one we followed.

title: narrō with a short a
decision: Write narrō, narrāre, not nārrō.
html: De Vaan (s.v. gnārus) derives the verb from *nārāre, shortened by the littera-rule, which Weiss calls the “narro rule”; de Vaan comes first where he discusses a vowel. Bennett’s nārrō rests on a single apex, NÁRREM in the Lyon tablet (CIL XIII 1668), on a syllable already long by position; in those inscriptions only about three apices in four stand on long vowels.

title: frūstrā with a long u
decision: Write frūstrā; frustum, “a piece”, is a different word, with a short u.
html: De Vaan (s.v. fraus) derives it from *fraud-tro-, and Bennett cites an apex (CIL VI 20370): both give a long u.

title: Short vowels before gn
decision: A vowel before gn is short unless its stem is long: magnus, signum, lignum, ignis, dignus, pugnus, pugna, but rēgnum (from rēx), stāgnum, sēgnis, abiēgnus.
html: This follows Bennett, Buck and Allen against the rule reported by Priscian that every vowel before gn is long. It is a deliberate exception to the precedence of de Vaan, whose pūgnus, pūgna (s.v. pungō) are not followed.

title: Perfect subjunctive -erīs, future perfect -eris
decision: The perfect subjunctive has a long ī (nē dīxerīs), the future perfect a short i (sī vēneris). A form that could be either is left short.
html: Bennett, and Allen and Greenough (§169.d), give the perfect subjunctive the long ī of the old optative. A clause drawn into a subjunctive clause counts as subjunctive (cum jūdicāverīs, Ps. 50:6 in Jerome’s psalter from the Hebrew); a general condition with a timeless present, or the polite grātum fēceris, stays short.

title: Clipped -ne keeps an apostrophe
decision: Write satin', vīn', ain', audīn', scīn', vidēn', with the vowel as long or short as in the base word.
html: The apostrophe marks the lost e of -ne. There is no compensatory lengthening: satin' keeps the short a of satis, audīn' the long ī of audīs. A following est keeps its e (satin' est, Ter. Ph. 210).

title: dēbeō is for duty
decision: dēbeō with an infinitive expresses duty or obligation; for what simply had to happen, use necesse est.
html: Lewis & Short: in classical prose it is always used of moral necessity.

title: jentāculum with a short e
decision: Write jentāculum and jentō with a short e.
html: Lewis & Short leaves the e unmarked, and no authority we follow marks it long.

title: linteum and mantēle
decision: The bath towel is linteum and the hand towel mantēle; a tablecloth is also linteum.
html: mantēle is the hand towel in Varro (L. 6.85) and Vergil (A. 1.702), and Martial uses lintea of a tablecloth (villōsa tegant tibi lintea citrum, 14.138). Traupman’s gausapina is classically a frieze coat, and manutergium is found only in Isidore.

title: Turning a tap on and off
decision: On: epitonium vertere. Off: epitonium claudere, or aquam sistere.
html: The verb is Varro’s (epitoniīs versīs, R. 3.5.16); compare Vergil’s sistere aquam fluviīs (A. 4.489). Traupman’s versāre and reversāre are not used: reversāre is late Latin. In narration, forms that do not sound the same in present and perfect are preferred (epitoniō versō, not vertit).

title: furcilla for the fork
decision: The table fork is furcilla, not fuscinula.
html: furcilla is a classical word (Varro, Cicero) whose table-fork sense is modern (Traupman 71). fuscinula occurs only in the Vulgate.

title: opus caementīcium for concrete
decision: Concrete is opus caementīcium, not Traupman’s concrētum.
html: After Vitruvius’s caementīcius.

title: exedra for the sitting room
decision: The sitting room is exedra, not sessōrium.
html: exedra is a room for sitting and conversation in Vitruvius and Cicero (Traupman 125). The ancient senses of sessōrium are “seat” and, in one passage of Petronius, “dwelling”.

title: gelātum for ice cream
decision: Ice cream is gelātum; Traupman’s congelidum crēmum and Morgan–Owens’s glaciēs dulcis are given as alternatives.
html: Antiquity had no ice cream to name, so the choice is between modern coinages. This one is the easiest to say, and it has modern precedent (Helfer; Vox Latina, both cited by the Neo-Latin Lexicon).

title: cedo with short vowels
decision: Cedo! “give it here” has a short e and a short final o, and its plural is cette.
html: Lewis & Short marks it cĕdo and lists it apart from cēdō, cēdere “go, give way”. It is an old imperative, from -ce and the root of dō.

title: lutra with a short u
decision: Write lutra, not Lewis & Short’s lūtra.
html: Lewis & Short gives no evidence for the long vowel, and its only etymological note, luō, has a short one. De Vaan (2008: 355) prints lutra and Proto-Italic *udrā-, from PIE *ud-ro- “of the water”, with the short u of Sanskrit udrá- and Greek ὕδρος. The long vowel of Lithuanian ūdra and Russian vydra comes from a Balto-Slavic lengthening (Winter’s law), which says nothing about Latin. Italian and Portuguese lontra and French loutre continue a short u; a long ū would have given u, as in luna and lune. The word occurs only in prose (Varro, Pliny), so verse cannot decide.

history.html: Cites Russian vydra, as de Vaan does, in place of a Bulgarian form: the lexicon is English–Latin.

title: fortasse with a short final e
decision: Write fortasse, not Lewis & Short’s fortassē.
html: Lewis & Short gives no evidence for the long vowel. De Vaan (2008: 236, s.v. fors) speaks of the word’s “short final vowel”, and verse proves it: in Catullus 85.1, Ōdī et amō. quārē id faciam fortasse requīris, the fifth foot, -tasse re-, must be a dactyl, so the e is short. Horace scans it the same way (S. 1.3.20, 1.6.98).

title: caccabus: a short a and a double c
decision: Write caccabus (also cacabus), not Lewis & Short’s cācabus.
html: The word is Greek κάκκαβος, with a short α and a double κ. Varro writes caccabum (cited by Lewis & Short), and Statius scans albōrum calicum atque caccabōrum (Silv. 4.9.45) with a heavy first syllable, which the double c explains. Lewis & Short’s cācabus marks that heavy syllable as a long vowel. Our Comenius quotation table still follows Lewis & Short.

title: mixtus with a short i
decision: Write mixtus, mixtōria, permixta without a macron on the i.
html: Traupman marks the i long, but Lewis & Short leaves it unmarked in mixtum, and de Vaan (2008: 382–383) prints mixtum, mixtūra with a short i, explaining mixtum as syncopated from *mixitum. Spanish mestizo and French métis, from Late Latin mixtīcius, also continue a short i. Bennett has not been checked yet.

title: oiei keeps its i
decision: Write oiei as Lewis & Short prints it, not ojei.
html: It is unclear whether the i’s of this interjection are vowels or consonants, so the j rule is not applied. The form also depends on the edition: the Perseus text of Terence does not print oiei at the places Lewis & Short cites. For a plain “ouch”, au is the better-attested word.

title: ōlla with a long o
decision: Write ōlla, ōllae with a long o.
html: ōlla is the later form of aula (Festus: aulās antīquī dīcēbant, quās nōs dīcimus ōllās), and an o that comes from au is long, as in cōda beside cauda and plōstrum beside plaustrum. Lewis & Short leaves the vowel unmarked; the quantity is hidden by the double l.

title: Modern place names: a convention for their vowels
decision: Where a modern place name has no Latin quantity to follow, mark the vowel that puts the Latin stress where the local stress falls: Alfāma (Alfama), Lisbōna (Lisboa). Nothing in history settles these vowels either way, so this is a convention that keeps the name recognisable, not a claim about how it was said.
html: A long vowel is the lightest way to make a light penult carry the stress. The convention does not choose between names: where a place has a Latin name of its own, the lexicon gives it beside the modern one, and either may be used (Lisbōna or Olisīpō, Conimbrica or Aeminium). Where a name has its own Latin quantities, they stand.

title: heri with a short final i
decision: Write heri, not herī: the classical word has a short final vowel, shortened from an older herī.
html: The word is an old locative. De Vaan (283) explains heri as shortened from an older *herī after its light first syllable, as in mihi, tibi, modo; the long herī that Terence has once is generally explained as made on domī and rūrī. The other form, here, has an old short vowel; Quintilian says that in it neither e nor i is clearly heard (1.4.8), and that it was the spelling of his day (1.7.22). Lewis & Short gives hĕri. Traupman 89 prints herī, and the house wrote it so until this ruling.

title: sēsqui- with a long e
decision: Write sēsquihōra, and sēsqui- in its other compounds, with a long e: the prefix is sēmis, “a half”, with -que.
html: De Vaan (553, s.v. sēmi-) derives sēsque- from *sēmis-que, “and a half”, and lists it beside sēstertius and sēlībra; the long ē of sēmi- stayed when the syllable after it was lost. Lewis & Short gives the same derivation (“contr. from semis-qui”) but leaves the vowel unmarked. Verse cannot show the length, since the syllable is heavy either way. Bennett (§52) marks it long too, with the same derivation, and Traupman 87 prints sēsquihōra.

title: Lachmann’s law: āctus, lēctus, frāctus
decision: A participle in -tus from a root ending in g has a long vowel: āctus, lēctus, rēctus, tēctus, tāctus, frāctus, and pāctus from pangō. Their derivatives keep it: āctiō, lēctiō, tēctum, dēlēctus, frāctūra.
html: By Lachmann’s law a short vowel was lengthened where a voiced stop met the t of the participle: agō, āctus; legō, lēctus; regō, rēctus; tegō, tēctus; tangō, tāctus; frangō, frāctus; and with d, cadō, cāsus; videō, vīsus; edō, ēsus. Gellius (9.6.3) says that āctitō is pronounced with a long first syllable because āctus is. Lewis & Short leaves most of these vowels unmarked. De Vaan names the law for frāctus (239) and for lēctus, rēctus, tāctus and tēctum. Bennett (The Latin Language §46.3) lists each of them long on its own evidence, and the house has written them so from the start. The law does not act before a voiceless stop or an old aspirate, so faciō, factus; dīcō, dictus; vehō, vectus; trahō, tractus are short (Bennett prints trāctus; W. S. Allen corrects it to trăctus), and so is pactum, which belongs to pacīscor. A few participles stay short against it, fictus, pictus, strictus, scissus and fissus among them; de Vaan (s.v. scindō) reports three explanations.

title: re- short before sc, sp, st
decision: Write respondeō, restō, respiciō, rescrībō with a short e in the prefix, against Lewis & Short’s rē-.
html: Lewis & Short marks the prefix long before s and a consonant (64 headwords), and does the same only for dis- (dī-scindō). Its reason is a lengthening to make up for the lost d of red-: its article on the prefix explains the poets’ rēdūcō by “the suppression of the d”. But Latin shows no such lengthening where a d is lost before s elsewhere, and Lewis & Short itself leaves a-scendō, a-spiciō and di-stō unmarked. Bennett (§48) rejects the idea as “an untenable theory of compensatory lengthening”; Lewis’s own Elementary Latin Dictionary (1890) prints re-spondeō; de Vaan (516) takes red- as the secondary form; Traupman writes respondēre. The syllable is heavy either way, so verse cannot decide.

title: ustus with a short u
decision: Write ustus and its compounds and derivatives (adustus, ambustiō, adustiō) with a short u.
html: Bennett (§52) gives ūrō, ussī, ūstus, the long vowel of the participle “according to the Romance”. Michelson’s note on Bennett allows the short vowel for Classical Latin; the zero grade of the root would be short; de Vaan prints ustum; Lewis & Short, Traupman and Morgan–Owens leave it unmarked; and the house’s readers have always written adustus, perustus and praeustus. The evidence for the long vowel is late and indirect, so the short vowel stands. It is a weak ruling: better evidence for ūstus should reopen it.

title: vēndō with a long ē
decision: Write vēndō, vēndere, vēndidī, vēnditum and its family (vēnditor, vēnditiō, vēnditāre, dīvēndō) with a long ē.
html: Contracted from vēnum dō (de Vaan 663, s.v. vēnum); Spanish keeps a close vowel, vendo beside tiendo from tendō; Traupman prints vēnditiō. Lewis & Short leaves the vowel unmarked. Quotations are marked to match.

title: ōrdō, ōrnō and ōrdior with a long ō
decision: Write ōrdō, ōrdinis, ōrdināre, ōrdinārius, ōrnāre, ōrnātus, ōrnāmentum, ōrdior, exōrdium, prīmōrdium with a long ō.
html: De Vaan (434) heads the entries ōrdior and ōrdō and prints ōrdināre, ōrdinārius, ōrnāre, ōrnātus, ōrnāmentum, adōrnāre, exōrnāre, subōrnāre; the long vowel is secondary, he says, as in other words with a vowel before r and a consonant (Leumann 1977: 114). Lewis & Short leaves the vowels unmarked, as it does before two consonants.

title: fūstis with a long ū
decision: Write fūstis and fūstīgāre with a long ū.
html: De Vaan (253) heads the entry fūstis and writes the word so throughout; Traupman prints it long. Lewis & Short leaves it unmarked.

title: jūrgō and objūrgō with a long ū
decision: Write jūrgō, jūrgium, objūrgō, objūrgātiō with a long ū.
html: De Vaan (316, s.v. jūs) prints jūrgium and explains jūrgāre, with Plautus’s spelling (ob)jūrigāre, from a noun *jūrago-. Lewis & Short itself gives the old form objūrigō with the long vowel, though it leaves jurgō unmarked.

title: rixa with a short i
decision: Write rixa and rixārī with a short i.
html: De Vaan (525) heads the entry rixa, prints rixārī, and derives the word from a zero-grade *rik-s-. Lewis & Short leaves the vowel unmarked. De Vaan takes precedence where he gives a quantity.

title: nōngentī and ūndēvīgintī
decision: Write nōngentī, nōngentēsimus with a long ō, and ūndecim, ūndēvīgintī, ūndētrīgintā with a long ū.
html: nōn- is the stem of nōnus, and Lewis & Short itself prints the older nōningentī; ūn- is ūnus. Lewis & Short leaves both unmarked before two consonants.

title: octō with a long final ō
decision: Write octō.
html: The inherited form, with the long vowel of Greek ὀκτώ; Traupman (253) prints it so. Lewis & Short’s octŏ is a shortened form.

title: lepōs with a long ō in the nominative
decision: Write the nominative lepōs (also lepor), genitive lepōris.
html: Like honōs and arbōs, the old nominative in -ōs keeps its long vowel. Lewis & Short prints lĕpos.

title: psȳchiāter and archiāter with a short i
decision: Write psȳchiāter, psȳchiātrīa, archiāter, paediāter with a short i before the long ā.
html: Lewis & Short marks the i short in archĭātrus and ĭātralipta; Greek ἰατρός is found with either quantity. The lexicon follows Lewis & Short.

title: Vowels Lewis & Short marks common
decision: A vowel Lewis & Short marks common (long or short) is left unmarked: Nēreis, Nēreidēs, terebra, cochlea, icō, icere. corōna is the exception and is written long.
html: The same rule as for biblical names. corōna keeps its macron because the Greek is κορώνη.

history.html: Applied to terebra (Lewis & Short tĕrē̆bra), cochlea (cō̆chlĕa) and the present of icō, icere (ī̆cĭo, ī̆co); the entries had given the first two in both forms and the third with a long vowel. The perfect īcī stays long.

title: caffea with a short e
decision: Write caffea, caffeae for coffee, as Traupman prints it, and so caffea expressa and caffea spūmōsa. Morgan–Owens’s caffēa is noted as a variant.
html: Traupman (70, 293) prints caffea -ae f. and caffeārius with no long vowel in the stem. Morgan–Owens (s.v. coffee) writes cafêa and caffêa, with a long e, citing Bartal. The word is modern and has no ancient quantity to follow. The entry had Morgan–Owens’s caffēa while the examples had Traupman’s caffeae.

title: impār, dispār and compār with a long ā
decision: Write the nominatives impār, dispār and compār with a long ā, as pār. The other cases are short: imparis, disparī.
html: Lewis & Short marks pār long and leaves the nominatives of its compounds unmarked (impar, dis-par, com-par). De Vaan (444, s.v. pār) prints compār, dispār and impār, and Traupman (150, 297) impār esse. The entry for an odd number had impar; the other entries had the long vowel.

title: prendō with a short e
decision: Write prendō, prendere, prendī, prēnsum.
html: Lewis & Short gives the contracted form of prehendō without a mark. De Vaan (487, s.v. prehendō) prints “contracted prendō” and the compounds apprendere, compre(he)ndere, dēpre(he)ndere and repre(he)ndere. The vowel is long only before ns: prēnsum, prēnsō, dēprēnsus. The entry had prēndō.

title: vīscus, vīscera with a long ī
decision: Write vīscus, vīsceris and the plural vīscera with a long ī. viscum, mistletoe and birdlime, is another word and keeps its short i.
html: Lewis & Short leaves viscus, -eris unmarked. De Vaan (683) heads the entry vīscus, -eris and prints vīscerātim and ēvīscerāre; on the same page he heads viscum, mistletoe, with a short i.

title: compescō with a short e
decision: Write compescō, compescere, compescuī.
html: Lewis & Short leaves the vowel unmarked. De Vaan (445, s.v. parcō) lists compescere and dispescere among the derivatives, with a short e. Traupman prints compēscō (291) and compēsce mentem (101, 336), which the entries had followed.

title: abdōmen with a long ō
decision: Write abdōmen, abdōminis.
html: Lewis & Short’s headword is abdŏmĕn. Verse shows the vowel long. In Juv. 4.107, Montānī quoque venter adest abdōmine tardus, which Lewis & Short itself cites, and in Juv. 2.86, atque bonam tenerae plācant abdōmine porcae, -dōmine is the dactyl of the fifth foot; its first syllable is open, so only a long vowel fills the place. De Vaan (20) heads the entry abdōmen. The ruling was for abdōmen once the verse had been checked; both lines were read in the LASLA text of Juvenal.

title: āëra, āëria with a diaeresis
decision: Write the forms of āēr and its derivatives with a diaeresis wherever the e is short: āëris, āëra, āëre, āërius, āëria, āëroplanum. The nominative āēr has a macron on its e and needs none.
html: The a and the e are two syllables (Lewis & Short āēr, āĕris, Greek ἀήρ), and the diaeresis keeps āëris, of the air, apart from aeris, of bronze, where ae is a diphthong. This is the house spelling; a few entries and quotations had been written without it (āera, āeria, āeris).

title: līctor with a long ī
decision: Write līctor, līctōris.
html: Lewis & Short’s headword is unmarked, but its article says “pronounced līctor, Gell. 12, 3, 4”. Gellius (12.3.4), who derives the word from ligāre against Tiro’s derivation from līcium, grants that prīma syllaba in “līctōre”, sīcutī in “līciō”, prōducta est et in eō verbō quod est “ligō” correpta est, and answers that līctor from ligandō, lēctor from legendō, vītor from viendō, tūtor from tuendō and strūctor from struendō were all made prōductīs quae corripiēbantur vōcālibus, with vowels lengthened that were short. He names the vowel, so this is evidence for its length and not only for a heavy syllable. De Vaan (341, s.v. ligō) prints līctor. Gellius was read in J. C. Rolfe’s text (1927), as the Perseus Digital Library gives it; vītor there is Lachmann’s correction of the manuscripts.

title: mūcrō with a long ū
decision: Write mūcrō, mūcrōnis.
html: Lewis & Short prints mucro without a mark, and the vowel stands before cr, where a heavy syllable in verse does not prove it long. De Vaan (391) heads the entry mūcrō, and the Latinitas loci collections write it so (Ambrose’s hymn Aeterne rērum, 23).

title: acroāma with a short first a
decision: Write acroāma, acroāmatis.
html: Lewis & Short’s headword is ācrŏāmă, with a long first vowel, beside the Greek it gives as its source, ἀκρόαμα, whose first vowel is short; it prints ācrŏāsis in the same way. The ruling follows the Greek.
